segments.text: A garment closure once cost hours of handwork. Machines dropped a meter of zipper to a few
grams of brass and tape. This is First Principles Daily, Episode 75. In the 1890s, closing
a boot still meant a row of tiny hooks and eyes. The same was true of a skirt and of
a tobacco pouch. Each hook was formed separately. Each eye was formed separately. A person set
every one of those pieces by hand, and every one of them was ready to snag the fabric, or to pop
open the first time the cloth was pulled sideways. The metal in that row was almost nothing, a pinch
of brass on a strip of cotton. But the fastener cost what the hands cost, and the hands were slow. A Swedish
American engineer named Gideon Sundbach looked at that row and refused to treat the row as a sowing
problem. By the early 1920s, automatic stamping and wire forming machines were turning out a meter of
interlocking teeth so cheaply that the price of the closure sat close to the price of the brass and the
tape themselves. That drop did not come from a better hook. The drop came from throwing the hook away. To see
why that was hard, you have to sit with the old way first, because the old way felt finished. For most of
the 19th century, a closable opening in cloth was a solved problem in the way that most solved problems
are solved. People copied the last thing that worked, buttons and buttonholes, laces through eyelets, hooks and
eyes sewn on in facing pairs. Each of those conventions assumed that a closure was a series of discrete
joints. A human being would fasten those joints one by one every time the garment went on. The joint
itself was cheap metal, or bone, or shell. The expense lived in the stitching, in the alignment, and in the
minutes the wearer spent doing up the row. Costs sat in time, not in metal. Whitcom L. Judson's class blocker
patented in 1893 and shown at the world's Columbian exposition in Chicago was the first serious attempt to
put a slider on that idea. The class blocker was still a hook and eye fastener. Two facing ranks of metal
hooks and eyes were meant to be drawn together by a movable guide, so the wearer would not have to
mate each pair with their fingers. The automatic hook and eye company, and later the universal fastener
company, tried to sell the device for shoes and pouches. The convention those companies inherited was
the convention they kept. The fastening elements were still individual hooks and individual eyes.
Those elements were still made and still attached as separate pieces. There were still few
enough of them per inch that a sideways tug could peel them apart. The slider was an accessory on
on top of a hand-built chain, not a reason to rethink the chain. That is why the default survived
even after someone had invented a pull tab. A factory that already knew how to stamp a hook and sew
the hook onto tape had no reason by analogy to throw the hook away. Each element could be inspected,
each element could be replaced. The part count was high and the assembly was manual, but the method
looked like clothing manufacturer and clothing manufacturer was what the customers and the investors
understood. Finished cost was dominated by labor and by scrap from misfitting pairs. A short run of
glass blocker that failed in the field did not merely waste the brass. Judson's design failed
often, popping open under lateral load, jamming when a hook sat a fraction off pitch. Failure wasted
the hours that had gone into setting every hook. Everyone inside the trade accepted that a reliable
automatic closure was, if such a closure was possible at all, a luxury item. The assumption baked
in was simple and almost invisible. A fastener is a row of little fasteners. Nobody had yet asked what
the row was made of or what a machine would do if the little fasteners were allowed to become one
repeating shape. Sunback refused that assumption. Working at the automatic hook and eye plant in
Hoboken in the years after 1966, Sunback did not start from the class blocker and tweaked the hook.
Sunback started from the job. Two edges of cloth must be joined and unjoined along a line.
Many times, without the joint peeling open when the cloth is pulled apart. The raw facts are a length,
a tensile load, and a handful of metal. Wave a magic wand, arrange the atoms, and the theoretical
floor for a meter of closure is the commodity value of a few grams of brass plus a narrow ribbon of
cotton tape. That is the magic wand number for this object. Brass is copper and zinc. Both copper
and zinc were ordinary industrial metals even then. Cotton tape was a textile commodity. A rough
magic wand estimate then and now is that the materials in a meter of metal zipper are worth a
trivial fraction of what a person costs for an hour. Penies in modern money, a similarly small slice
of a worker's wage in 1915. Anything you pay above that floor is design, handling, and process.
That gap is the idiot index in plain language. Finnist price divided by the value of the stuff inside.
Take a hand-built hook and eye chain, whose selling price was set by assembly time, not by brass.
Forming, pairing, aligning, and sewing dozens of separate elements on a short length of tape
so clearly swamped the metal that a back of the envelope pass puts the ratio in the tens
and very plausibly higher. Nobody published a measured ratio. The arithmetic is still visible
without one. If the brass and the cotton are pennies and the selling price is the price of an hour
of fussy handwork, the finished thing costs many times the materials. A high ratio of that kind is not
a law of fasteners. A high ratio is a signal that the design is still a sewing problem.
Sunbacks answer was five moves, and none of them required a new element from the periodic table.
The first move was to throw away the idea of paired, dissimilar elements. Hooks and eyes are two
different parts that have to find each other. Sunback replaced those two shapes with a single repeating
scoop. Every tooth on both sides of the chain is the same shape. A machine that only has to make
one shape can run without changing dies, without sorting left from right, and without a human checking
that a hook faces an eye. The chain becomes a continuous rank of identical units, which is the
form that stamping and wire forming want. Part count per meter does not fall in the sense that there
are fewer teeth. There are more teeth, but the number of kinds of part collapses, and the number
of assembly decisions collapses with it. That is what lets cost slide toward the metal. One shape,
one die, one repeating motion. The second move was the geometry of the scoop itself. The design that
appears in sunbacks 1917 United States patent for a separable fastener. Each tooth carries a pocket
on one face and a rounded projection on the other, when the two ranks mesh, every projection sits in
the opposing pocket. Here is the physics that Judson's hooks never had. A sideways pull, the exact
load that peeled a clasp blocker open, now drives the projection deeper into the pocket instead of
prying the joint apart. Peel becomes lock. The chain is no longer a series of independent latches.
The chain is a single shear resistant structure whose strength scales with how many scoops are
engaged. Sunback also packed more elements into each inch than the old hook and eye ranks had used.
Finer pitch means each tooth takes less load. The slider runs more smoothly. A missing or damaged
tooth is less likely to open a gap. The tradeoff that had to be won was pitch accuracy. If the spacing
wanders, the projections miss the pockets and the slider jams. The design only works if the
manufacturing process can place every scoop on a strict interval. That is why the machine and the
tooth were one invention, not two. You cannot buy the geometry first and invent the factory later.
The third move was to stop attaching the fastener to the garment and start attaching the fastener to a
tape. The cloth ribbon, the stringer, became a standardized backbone. Teeth are clenched onto the
tape in a factory that never sees the coat or the tent. A garment maker then soars the finished
chain into a seam, the way that maker would sew on a binding. That decoupling is easy to skip past,
and it is one of the reasons the cost fell. As long as each hook was sewn to the actual shoe or
corset, fastener manufacturer was trapped inside garment manufacturer, at garment shop speed,
with garment shop labor. Once the product is a roll of chain, the product can be made continuously,
inventory by the meter and sold to anyone. The tape also spreads the load from each tooth into the cloth
along a sewn length rather than at a single stitch. That is why a modern zipper can take a hard
yank without ripping out one element at a time. The joint stopped being a row of stitches and became
a sewn length. The fourth move was the machine that made the third move real. Sunbacks equipment fed
metal wire and cotton tape and emitted finished stringer. In one repeating cycle, the wire is cut and
formed into a scoop, and the scoop is clenched onto the edge of the tape at the required pitch.
There is no bin of pre-made hooks. There is no alignment jig for pairing. There is no thread
tying each element on. Wire is the cheap form of the alloy, drawn in long runs, uniform in section,
ready to be headed and formed. The clinch is a mechanical joint that needs no solder and no adhesive.
Scrap still exists. Stamping and forming are never perfectly net shape, but the handling steps that
had multiplied the idiot index are gone. A single machine running a single motion replaced a room of
people doing fussy repetitive work, and the machine did so at a consistency no assembler could hold
for an hour. The objection at the time would have been that a machine that precise would itself be
expensive, and early special purpose equipment always is. The answer is volume. Once the chain is
a commodity measured in meters, the capital cost of the machine is amortized across an enormous
length of brass and tape. That is exactly the arithmetic that drops the finished meter toward
the magic wand floor. Pay for the machine once. Spread that payment over kilometers of identical
scoops. The fifth move was the slider, redesigned as a small cam rather than a loose guide.
The body of a zipper slider is a y-shaped channel. Two ranks of teeth enter the arms of the y.
A wedge and a pair of rails force those ranks into mesh. The ranks leave the stem as one chain,
pull the other way, and the wedge does the reverse. That geometry converts a single linear pull into
a sequence of engagements, which is the whole point of not fastening each pair by hand.
The slider is the one part of a zipper that is still relatively speaking, a mechanism. A stamped or
die-cast body, a pull tab, sometimes a lock. The slider is also the part whose idiot index stayed
higher than the chains, because a slider is a three-dimensional object with internal surfaces
that have to be accurate. Even so, making one slider per garment is a different cost structure from
making and setting 40 hooks. The trade-off here was where, and the tendency of a poorly fitted slider
to chew the teeth or to ride up over them. Brass helped. Brass is formidable. Brass bears against
itself without galling the way some steals will. Brass does not rust in the pocket of a coat.
Later alloys and plated zinc die-castings chased the same properties at lower cost,
but the first principal's choice was already visible in 1917. Pick the metal that wants to be
formed and that will slide on itself, not the metal that looks strongest on a data sheet.
Five moves, identical scoops instead of hooks and eyes. Pocket and projection geometry that turns
peel into lock. A tape backbone that lets the factory ignore the garment. A wire to stringer
machine that holds pitch and clinches in one cycle. A wide channel slider that is a cam, not a loose
guide. None of those five required a new atom. Those five required refusing the analogy that a closure
is a row of little closures, and then building a process whose natural output is a continuous,
identical load-sharing chain. The magic wand floored to not change. The idiot index did,
because almost everything that was not brass or cotton was designed out. By the 1920s the automatic
machines had done what that redesigned promised. The machines reduced the cost of a meter of closure
to something that sat near the price of a few grams of brass and a strip of cotton tape.
Exact factory gate figures from those years are not something the public record hands us with any
confidence, and it would be dishonest to invent those figures. What is clear is the direction and the
scale. A product that had been too unreliable and too labor-heavy to leave a niche in shoes and
pouches, became cheap enough and smooth enough to put on rubber boots. B.F. Goodrich's 1923 zipper
boot is what gave the device its common name. Then the same chain went on to jackets, tents, luggage,
and flight suits. The hookless fastener company became Tallinn. Decades later YKK built the same logic
out to a global, vertically integrated extreme, widely reported to account for a very large share of
world zipper output, in some accounts around half, by making its own alloys, its own tapes,
and its own machines. That is what a collapsed idiot index looks like when someone keeps pushing.
A modern commodity metal or coil zipper, bought in bulk, often sells for well under a dollar,
and sometimes for a few tens of cents. The materials are still a few grams of brass, aluminum,
acetal, or nylon, plus a polyester tape, worth cents or less at commodity prices.
Walk the ratio out loud if the stuff inside is worth cents, and the finished zipper sells for
tens of cents or a fraction of a dollar, the finished price is only a handful of times the materials,
maybe into the load tens on a branded retail spare. That is a rough, fully visible estimate,
not a measured factory audit. Compare that handful, or those load tens, with the crushing multiple of
the hand assembled era, when labor and pairing and scraps set the price. The remaining gap on a
basic zipper is mostly the slider, plating, or coating, the sewing allowance on the tape,
packaging, and the logistics of selling a small object. Specialty closures are a different story.
Waterproof and airtight zippers, the kind used on dry suits and some outdoor gear,
still carry a much higher ratio, because sealing lips, tighter tolerances, and lower volumes
put the process cost back in charge. The physical floor did not rise, the design left the floor.
Honest limits remain. A zipper is a mixed material object, metal or acetal teeth, textile tape,
a die cast, or molded slider, and a zipper is miserable to recycle as a unit. A zipper jams when a thread
enters the slider, which is a geometric fact about a y-shaped channel, not a manufacturing error.
A zipper is hard to repair in the field compared with a button. Coil and molded plastic chains took
the materials bill even closer to the floor than brass did, but those chains did it by accepting
a lower melting point and a different failure mode. The first principles win was real, and that win
was mostly complete for the ordinary case by the time the machines of the 1920s were running.
What is left is not a secret about brass. What is left is the unglamorous work of seals, recycling,
and the last expensive part in the assembly, the slider. Two things travel from Hoboken. The first
is that a row of little parts is almost never the cheapest way to make a line. Sunbacks identical
scoops clinched at a machine pitch onto a tape, replace the census of hooks and eyes because one
repeating motion is what wire forming actually wants to do. Stamping does not want to hook in an eye
and a pairing step. Stamping wants one shape over and over at a pitch the die can hold. If you are
the second thing that travels is that the joint and the factory have to be designed as a pair.
The pocket and projection tooth only pays off once a machine can hold the interval. The tape
only pays off once the fastener is allowed to be a roll of chain instead of a step in a tailor's
shop. Design the tooth without the process and the slider jams. Design the process without changing
the product and you are still sewing on hooks. Process and design were one invention. That pairing is
the portable piece. Wherever a continuous job is still being done by a census of little parts,
look at the magic wand floor, the raw atoms, the commodity tape, the drawn wire, and then look at
how many times the finished price exceeds those atoms. A high multiple is not proof that the materials
are expensive. A high multiple is often proof that the design is still a sewing problem and that nobody
has yet let the machine emit the joint it wants to emit. The question worth carrying out the door
is simple. Where else are we still sewing on hooks, one by one, because that is what a closure has
always looked like. That's first principles daily for today. If this changed how you see what
things cost, share it with someone who depreciate it and subscribe wherever you listen. I'm Patrick
and Vancouver, one example or one opportunity every day. See you tomorrow and if you'd rather watch
